runs.text: Hum vaſo que ſerue no Chanoyu pera

lines.note: Gesui denotes a tea-ceremony vessel for discarded water; the next lines extend the name to its contents. The final ui is visible, correcting Gueſu; Chanoyu occurs inside the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: vazar nelle agoa: mas mais propriamente ſe

lines.note: The vessel receives poured-out water. Nelle and the colon after agoa are visible; the following contrast introduces the more specific sense of the headword.

runs.text: toma pella agoa que esta neſte vaſo.

lines.note: The word is more properly applied to the water in this vessel. Esta is retained without supplying a modern accent or changing the historical spelling pella.

runs.text: Hũs chiripos feitos ao modo de Iapão

lines.note: Geta are described by comparison with Japanese-style low footwear. The weak nasal marks and damaged country-name are read as Hũs and Iapão; the gloss does not warrant a modernized name for the footwear.
Muito baixos completes the description of the geta as very low. The marks after the period are stray ink rather than an additional lexical item.
Geten is explained by ten yori kudaru, descending from heaven. The visible final label is retained as Bur., without silently regularizing it to the more familiar Buddhist abbreviation Bup.
Guetjen is paraphrased as tsuki no mae, before the moon. The printed t before j is retained as part of the historical romanization rather than expanded within the transcription.
Gekkwo is moonlight, as tsuki no hikari confirms. The scan supports Guetquǒ rather than Cuatquǒ; this entry starts indented in the impression, unlike the surrounding flush-left headwords.
Da lũa completes claridade, the moon's brightness. It belongs to Guetquǒ and remains a separate physical row.
Geshakubara is equated with sobabara and glossed as an illegitimate child. The initial is G, not OCR C; the following example explains the family relationship.
The phrase geshakubara no ko repeats the headword with child. The Portuguese explicitly supplies illegitimate; the native impression joins Guexacubarano and leaves a word space before co.

runs.text: ou que não he fiho da propria molher.

lines.note: The child is not the son of the man's own wife. The impression appears to omit l in fiho; that printed anomaly is retained rather than silently repairing it to filho.
Gesen means baseness or a person of low standing. Baixo belongs entirely to the italic Portuguese gloss, not to an isolated roman a as in the OCR styling.
Gesenna gives the corresponding adjectival expression for something or someone low. The damaged internal letter in the final baixo is read with the matching form immediately above.
This gesetsu entry concerns something low or vile, or baseness itself. Keep it distinct from the separate homographic entry about popular speech below.

runs.text: O falar, ou contar de gente baixa.

lines.note: The second gesetsu denotes the speech or accounts of common people. Its separate headword is printed and should not be merged with the preceding entry.

Gesetsu ni koo yuu means that people commonly say this. Aſsi restores the word for thus; po- begins povo below. The marker retains the aligned draft's mixed styling: its capital V is upright, while the following t is more slanted; the tiny type makes that distinction less secure than the words.

runs.text: uo, ou em pratica da gente popular.

lines.note: Completes povo and explains the expression as something said in ordinary people's discourse. Pratica, not OCR pratca, supplies the missing visible i.
Geshi is explained as reaching summer; the Portuguese describes the start of summer. The scan supports Principio, while the calendar specification continues below.

runs.text: ou estio. i, no meyo da quinta lũa.

lines.note: The entry places this seasonal point in the middle of the fifth lunar month. Preserve that historical calendrical explanation instead of replacing it with a modern calendar date.
This geshi denotes a tusk, explained by kiba and ha. The Portuguese names the wild boar first; mõ- continues into the adjective on the next line.
Completes mõtes, describing a wild boar, and adds the elephant's tusk. The final letter is s, not the OCR's r; the historical spelling elephante is preserved.

runs.text: Superior mediato, ou official que esta

lines.note: Another geshi is an intermediate superior or subordinate official. The visible word official restores the OCR's missing initial o; the relative clause continues below.
The official is under another authority. De baixo is printed as separate words and is not to be modernized into debaixo.
Geshi, gesuru, geshita is a Buddhist verb for becoming clear or freed from passions. Bup. is an upright domain label; li- begins the Portuguese verb livrar on the following row.

runs.text: urarſe das paixoens cõ as meditaçoens do Bup

lines.note: Completes livrar-se and attributes release from passions to Buddhist meditation. Bup at the edge continues as po below; the scan has neither the OCR's extra e nor a clearly printed terminal hyphen.
Po completes Buppo in the Portuguese explanation; kokoro wo gesuru illustrates clarification or liberation of the heart. Preserve the physical split and the upright Japanese example.

runs.text: Homem que esta preſo, ou conde-

lines.note: Geshinin is a person imprisoned or condemned in another's place. The scan supports the headword's initial G; conde- begins condenado across the next row.

runs.text: nado em lugar de outro que he o proprio reo,

lines.note: Completes condenado and distinguishes the substitute prisoner from the actual defendant. This relative clause belongs to the same definition.

runs.text: poſtoque ordinariamente ſe ſalua por inculpa-

lines.note: The definition adds that the substitute is ordinarily released as innocent. Inculpa- is a genuine line-end division, completed below.
Geshinin wo dasu, alternatively hiku, means providing someone in one's place. Latin l marks the alternative verb; Dar begins the Portuguese explanation.

runs.text: o reo alguem em ſeu lugar.

lines.note: The defendant supplies another person as a substitute. This completes Dar above and explains who performs the action in the Japanese example.
Geshoo is explained by toki and kiyuru, dissolving or disappearing. The circumflex is retained and is distinct from the caron on the following low-birth entry.

Koori geshoo su describes ice melting. The printed example contains one circumflexed o, not OCR's doubled marked vowels; caramelo has the contextual sense ice here, and ocaramelo retains its tight printed joining.
This geshoo is low birth, paraphrased as an inherently low condition. Preserve its caron rather than copying the circumflex from the adjacent homograph; Bai- begins baixo.
Completes baixo nacimento and restates it as low lineage. Nacimento is the printed historical spelling and is not expanded to modern nascimento.
The next geshoo denotes the lower parts of the body. The example and contrasting upper and middle regions belong to this anatomical entry.
Geshoo no hiyeta is glossed as the lower parts becoming cold. The first letters are Gue-, not OCR Ciue-; keep the printed no construction rather than rewriting the Japanese.
After completing the lower-parts example, jooshoo names the upper regions. Its first o bears a caron and the second a circumflex; co- leads into como below.

The head exemplifies the upper region; chuushoo introduces the middle region. The mark over u is a single oblique stroke, read as a grave, while the final o bears a circumflex. These are not regularized from vowel length.
The middle parts include the belly. This completes the three-way lower, upper, and middle division without introducing another headword.
Geshoku is a lowly occupation or service. Geshoku suru supplies the verbal example, divided after su- at the column edge.
Ru completes suru; the Portuguese means performing a lowly task or occupation. The break is retained rather than joining the Japanese across rows.
Gesshoku is glossed here as the moon's colour or appearance, as tsuki no iro confirms. Preserve the doubled x and do not substitute a different modern sense suggested by the pronunciation.
Aparencia completes the alternative description of the moon's appearance. The final S. marks written usage rather than another word in the gloss.
Geyaku is a subordinate office, literally shita no yaku. The initial G and final o of Officio are visible in the native crop.
Inferior completes the description of a subordinate office. It replaces OCR poſerior; the upright X. is the regional usage label, not part of the italic adjective.

zones.label: Printed page number
zones.note: The first numeral is damaged or overprinted; 117 is retained from its surviving form and the adjacent leaf sequence.

lines.note: Geyoo denotes the rice provisions of people of low standing. Shita-jita no hanmai supplies the Japanese paraphrase; Mantimen- is a divided Portuguese word, not a sentence ending.

runs.text: to, ou comer darroz de gente baixa, ou arroz

lines.note: Completes mantimento and describes rice food for common people. Comer is continuous in the impression; the second arroz begins an alternative definition.

runs.text: ordinario, & mal pilado. No Ximo ſe diz

lines.note: The alternative is ordinary, poorly polished rice. The Portuguese then introduces a regional name in Ximo, a Japanese place-name embedded in the explanation.
Qeyoo is the regional equivalent introduced by se diz above. The initial is a capital Q with its surviving tail, not OCR D; the word belongs to the Portuguese naming construction.
Geza is the lower seat or place, equated with shimoza. Gue- begins the example gezani tsuku on the following line.
Gezani tsuku means taking the lowest seat. The Portuguese explicitly supplies sitting down; baxo retains the printed spelling without an inserted i.
The seating is in a zashiki. Zaxiqui is an upright Japanese noun within the Portuguese phrase do Zaxiqui, rather than a new headword or standalone example.

runs.text: Vſaſe às vezes ẽ lugar de Coto. i, couſa

lines.note: Gi can substitute for koto, thing or matter. Vſaſe restores the Portuguese verb; Coto is the Japanese term within the explanation. Only a minute speck follows couſa, so no final period is added to the aligned draft.

runs.text: Hum dos cinco primores, ou custumes

lines.note: A separate gi is one of five praised social virtues or customs. The enlarged space after cinco contains no securely printed comma; the following comma after primores is clear. Preserve the dictionary's characterization rather than substituting a modern definition.
The customs are described as celebrated among the Chinese and Japanese. The scan reads Iapoens, not OCR Iapoems; the explanation continues into its moral qualities.
The entry compares this virtue with humility and restraint. These are the compilers' explanatory choices and should not be replaced by a narrower modern gloss.
Moderation in everything completes the account of gi. The short row is ordinary body text within that definition.
Gyakuchi is perverse knowledge, paraphrased as sakashimana chie. The headword begins Guia-, not OCR Giua-; per- begins perverso.
Completes perverso, qualifying the knowledge in the preceding row. The historical u-for-v spelling and long s are preserved.
Gyakudoo is a wrong path, paraphrased as sakashimana michi. The initial sequence and caroned o are visible; cami- continues as caminho.
The bad path is interpreted as bad deeds. Gyakudoo wo okonoo illustrates performing them, with the verb divided after vo-.
Conǒ completes voconǒ, to perform. The Portuguese says to do bad deeds; its grave-marked màs is retained rather than modernized.

Gyakufuu is an adverse wind, explained as sakashimana kaze. The accent is read as a damaged caron: a weak left trace and rising right arm compare with the repeated marked u below. The left arm is fragmentary, so this remains a nonblocking graphic caveat rather than a normalization of all long-u signs.
Completes contrario and illustrates an adverse wind blowing: gyakufuu ga fuku. The scan supports the word followed by ga, not the OCR's malformed ffigai sequence.
The Portuguese translates the wind example, then begins a second illustration with Guia-. That fragment continues into the same headword on the next physical row.
Gyakufuu ni mo kunzu describes giving off a fragrance even against an adverse wind. The native crop shows a mark over u, absent from the baseline's cufunimo; the explanation continues below.

runs.text: contrario que leua o cheiro a outra parte.

lines.note: The wind carries the scent elsewhere, yet the fragrance is perceptible. S. marks this expression as written usage.
Gyakugi is a wrong or perverse matter, explained by sakashima no gi. Per continues below without a clearly printed line-end hyphen; no hyphen is supplied merely from the word's continuation.
Completes perversa cousa, a perverse thing or action. This short continuation belongs to Guiacugui.
Gyakugyoo denotes acting perversely, with sakashimani okonoo as its paraphrase. The scan supports Guia- and the caroned vowels rather than OCR Cui-.
The gloss specifies bad or perverse deeds, then contrasts jungyoo as good deeds. Iunguiǒ is a Japanese antonym, not a Portuguese word or a citation label.
Completes boas obras with right or upright deeds. This belongs to the contrasting Iunguiǒ sense introduced on the preceding row.
Gyakujun pairs opposition with compliance and is cross-explained by jungyaku. The capital I is visible in Iunguia-, correcting the OCR's initial long s; its continuation remains on the next line.
Cu completes Iunguiacu. The Portuguese pairs crooked and straight, then bad and good, explaining the two opposed elements rather than describing one uniformly bad quality.
Gyakushin is a treacherous heart or intention. Sakashima no kokoro and traição jointly establish the betrayal sense.
Gyakushin wo okosu means conceiving or plotting treachery. The Portuguese armar traição gives the action intended by the Japanese example.
Gyakushitsu is a disease of recurring fever, explained as okori no yamai. Retain the terminal t of the historical Sino-Japanese form; the symptoms continue below.
The gloss specifies agues, fevers and chills. It is a historical symptom description, not an identification of a particular modern pathogen.
Gyakushu is something done for the sake of one's future life or salvation. The headword's Guia- is visible; the following Portuguese explains the anticipatory rites.

runs.text: Obras pias, ou exequias, &c. que hum faz

lines.note: The entry names pious works or funeral observances that a person arranges. Faz governs fazer on the next row, expressing having the rites performed.

runs.text: fazer em vida pera ſua ſaluação, as quais lhe

lines.note: The rites are arranged during life for one's salvation. The scan clearly includes lhe, not the OCR's he; it connects to the rites others would perform for the person after death.

runs.text: auião de fazer de pois de ſua morte.

lines.note: These are rites that would otherwise have been performed after the person's death. Preserve the printed spacing de pois and historical auião.
Gyakuen is described as friendship, a good deed, or contact arising incidentally. Commu- is the start of communicação; OCR commur lost the physical continuation mark.

runs.text: nicação que não he de propoſito ſe não com al-

lines.note: The contact is not deliberately sought but arises on some occasion. Al- continues into the indefinite expression on the following row.
Completes algũa ocasião and begins gyakuen nagara tomuroo. The example applies the incidental relationship to commemorating a deceased person.
Murǒ completes tomurǒ. The Portuguese describes commending a deceased person in prayer by chance or incidentally.
The commemoration may arise on some occasion. The scan supports doubled cc and long s in occaſião, replacing the OCR's ocajião without modernizing the spelling.
Gyakuzai is a perverse fault or sin, paraphrased by sakashimana tsumi. The Portuguese begins its explanation with pecado.

runs.text: peruerſidade dalgũa couſa feita ao contrario

lines.note: The fault is doing something contrary to the proper course. Dalgũa retains its printed nasal mark rather than being expanded or modernized.
Completes the comparison: contrary to what should have been done. The relative clause closes Guiacuzai before the next fever term.
Gyahei is another term for an ague or recurring fever, explained by okori no wazurai. The scan supports initial Guia- and an actual terminal hyphen after de.
The gloss specifies tertian fevers or agues. The catchword beneath the text anticipates the next fever headword and must remain separate from this final body line.
